But precisely because he is a prophet, he cannot be the Seal of absolute walayat. Perhaps, working in a Sunni environment, Ibn Arabi felt obliged to conceal part of his belief, a practice known as ketman. Haydar Amoli spent many pages debating who should be called the Seal of walayat. We have already noted the question and need not pursue it further here (see note 247 and Book Four, Chapter One, below).

The correspondence—or, more exactly, the symmetry—between the cycles also depends on the titles given to two figures. The Prophet Muhammad is the final Seal of the prophets and of prophecy. The Twelfth Imam, who also bears the name Muhammad, is the future Seal of Muhammadan walayat and of God's Friends.

In him, Shiism expresses a profound conviction about its place in the future: it sees itself as the final spiritual fulfillment of the enduring prophetic religion shared by humanity. Accordingly, every person initiated into the cycle of walayat stands in relation to the Twelfth Imam—“now hidden from the senses, but present in the hearts of his followers”—as each prophet in the earlier cycle stood in relation to Muhammad, the Seal of Prophecy.

We have already seen that the idea of the “Seal of Prophecy” grows out of a teaching about prophecy that closely resembles that of the Jewish-Christian Ebionites. It recalls the Verus Propheta, the True Prophet, who passes from one prophet to another, “hastening toward the place of his rest.” There is, of course, an important difference. In the Islamic account, the final prophet—the one in whom all earlier prophets find their rest and fulfillment—is not Christ. It is Muhammad, who came after Christ and whom, according to an interpretation shared throughout Muslim Qur'anic commentary, Christ himself foretold.

We can picture these relationships in several ways. Imagine a circle divided into two halves. One half may be the arc of descent (qaws al-nozul): revelation coming down, the giving of scripture (tanzil), and prophecy. The other is the arc of ascent (qaws al-so'ud): the discovery of deeper meaning (ta'wil), the Imamate, and walayat. Or imagine the circle the other way around.

First comes the upward arc, rising toward the noon of prophecy in its fullest revelation. Then comes the downward arc, entering the night of hidden spiritual meaning until the dawn of spiritual Resurrection and the appearance of the Twelfth Imam. In either picture, the prophets and God's Friends (awliya) stand opposite their counterparts on the two arcs.

Alternatively, we can picture two complete, separate circles: one for the “cycle of prophecy” (da'irat al-nobowwat), the other for the “cycle of walayat” (da'irat al-walayat). Here too the corresponding positions of prophets and God's Friends are clear. Shamsoddin Lahiji (died 912 AH/1506 CE) suggests both diagrams in his great commentary on The Rose Garden of Mystery, by the celebrated mystic Mahmud Shabestari of Azerbaijan (died 720 AH/1317 CE). In one version, the circles face each other; in the other, a single circle has two arcs symbolizing a cosmic “Day” and “Night”—a full cycle of day and night in the life of the world.

In this image, the sequence of prophets traces a circle (da'ira, khatt mostadir) whose points are the prophets themselves. Adam's life marks the first point of the “cycle of prophecy” in our world. To say that prophecy first appeared (zohur) with Adam is to say that he was the first earthly manifestation of its eternal reality (haqiqat). Every prophet (nabi) who followed manifested that same eternal prophetic Reality in a particular form. The cycle reaches completion in Muhammad. Coming last, he manifests in his earthly person every perfection that the earlier prophets had revealed separately. He gathers them all together (jami'iyat, or anakephalaiosis): in him the original prophetic Reality appears in its fullness.

Once the cycle of prophecy ends, the cycle of spiritual initiation begins. It is now for the Imams, God's Friends and Beloved, to initiate their own friends and followers into prophecy's inner meaning. Certainly prophecy and initiation are both present in the Prophet himself.

Indeed, his walayat—his divinely given spiritual authority and closeness to God—is the very source of his prophetic mission, his nobowwat (see the diagram above, p. 259). But because he has been sent as a prophet, and specifically as a prophet who brings a sacred Law, his prophetic office and message (nobowwat and risalat) do not include a mission to reveal the hidden meaning of the religion whose outward wording he proclaims.

That is why prophecy and initiation are assigned to two persons: the Prophet and the Imam. As we already know, this distinction lies at the heart of Twelver Shiite teaching about the Imamate, whose full reality appears in the twelve persons of the Imams.

We must also remember what makes the cycle of initiation following the Seal of the Prophets unique. Before Muhammad, every prophetic age prepared for the arrival of another prophet. Now that prophecy has closed, the cycle of walayat will not end with a new prophet or a new established religion. It prepares instead for the appearing of the Hidden Imam. With him will come the unveiling of what has remained concealed in all earlier revelations. The cycle of initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy is therefore initiation in its pure form—walayat mahz, spiritual knowledge no longer preparing for a new outward Law. This is the basis of the correspondence between the two cycles.

We have already described this correspondence briefly. Just as the prophets before the Seal of Prophecy each manifested the same eternal prophetic Reality (haqiqat-e nobowwat), so the Friends of God, who guide and initiate others, manifest an eternal walayat: initiation into the inner meaning of prophecy. And just as the cycle of prophecy reached its completion in the Seal of the Prophets (Khatim al-Anbiya), so the cycle of initiation reaches its fulfillment in the Seal of the Initiated, the Seal of God's Friends (Khatim al-Awliya).

Two ideas give this Shiite vision of the last things its distinctive character. First, traditions traced back to the Prophet identify the Seal of God's Friends with the Hidden Imam, the Twelfth Imam, child of Imam Hasan Askari and Princess Narkes (see Book Seven below).

Second, the future appearing of the now-hidden Imam will reveal the divine truths and secrets (haqa'iq, asrar-e ilahi) concealed within the wording of earlier revelations and the commands of outward religion. His appearance will usher in the reign of ta'wil, the uncovering of inner meaning. It will free people from every form of bondage and torment imposed by the Law. Spiritual knowledge and divine wisdom prepare for, and already anticipate, this appearance whenever they uncover the hidden meaning. They will reach their fullest development when the Imam and Guide, the Mahdi, appears and brings the cycle of initiation to its close.

This also points to the spiritual meaning we should give to the “events of the end.” Shiite books describe them in their chapters on the last things with dramatic scenes and the “return” (raj'at) of great figures from earlier ages. We should read those accounts in this light. Consider, for example, the saying in which the Prophet announces the last Imam's coming:

Those who dwell in Heaven and those who dwell on Earth will recognize him. Heaven will hold back not a drop of its water, but will pour it out in life-giving rain. Earth will keep back not a single growing thing, but will make it sprout and flourish, until those then alive will wish for the dead to rise again.

And the very power of this wish will bring about that resurrection. The Imam and his companions will prepare it together; indeed, he has already begun the work through those who, generation after generation, are the “companions of the Hidden Imam.” As Lahiji says, the resurrection of the dead—the awakening of dead souls—is what makes it possible for the purpose and fruit of existence finally to be fulfilled. People will attain perfect knowledge and become true knowers of spiritual reality (arifan-e haqiqi). The Imam's reign will prepare the way for this magnificent new beginning.

Our writers know that philosophy allows for the possibility that the world might be destroyed. But their understanding of the Imam enables them to challenge that possibility. Iran's vision of the final destiny of the world has shown a striking continuity, both before and after Islam. In Zoroastrian teaching, salvation and the end of history center on frashkart: the transformation or renewal of the world through the Saoshyant and his companions, preparing for the final restoration of all things.

Shiite teaching about the last things is centered on the Resurrector (Qa'im) and his companions. It looks toward a new beginning (isti'naf), a new age, an apokatastasis: the restoration of all things to their original state of light. It does not separate the “lesser resurrection,” an individual's departure from the perishable body, from the “greater resurrection,” the coming of that new age.

Let us now look more closely at how the two Seals correspond, and how each relates to those who manifest its reality. Our authors explain that just as the Seal of the Prophets gathered into himself all the earlier prophets who had manifested the eternal prophetic Reality, the Seal of the Initiated gathers into himself every initiate, every Friend of God. The perfection present as a possibility throughout the cycle of initiation becomes fully real in his person.

All are related to him as members of a single mystical body (corpus mysticum). This is why the Sufi understanding of walayat would be left without a foundation if we removed the Shiite understanding of the Imam. It is not enough to say that the Prophet himself was the first bearer of walayat. In him, this walayat remains—and must remain—hidden. It can become openly active only through the Imam's work of spiritual initiation, embodied in the Imam himself.

We can ask another question. The title “Friends” or “Beloved of God” (awliya) belongs in a special sense to the Twelve Imams. How can their followers share in it? To understand this, we must picture a relationship like that between the prophet's mission and the Imam's work of initiation. Prophecy springs from walayat itself and is like the sun; the Imam's walayat draws its light from that sun, just as the moon draws its light from the sun.

The word wali can mean both the one who loves and the one who is loved. With this double meaning in mind, our authors call the initiatory role of the “Seal of the Initiated” a solar walayat (shamsiya). The walayat of every other initiate or Friend of God—from the Afrad to the Noqaba, different ranks among the spiritual guides—is lunar (qamariya).
The Twelfth Imam, as Seal of the Initiated, possesses and reveals the eternal reality of walayat (haqiqat-e walayat):

Absolute initiation, in the fullness of all its perfections, appears in his person. He is the Whole. All the other Initiated manifest only one of initiation's perfect qualities, and so are like parts in relation to the Seal of the Initiated. Because he is with all of them, he is with each one.

This becomes understandable only through the intimate relationship between the Seal of the Prophets and the Seal of the Initiated. And, for our authors, that relationship can be understood in its full depth only through Shiite teaching.

We can distinguish three ways in which one person may be another's child (farzandi): descent through the body, the bond of affection through the heart, and a spiritual relationship that is essential and true. Shiite writers argue that all three come together completely in the Twelfth Imam, and only in him. Because he embodies this threefold relationship, they can say:

In truth, the Seal of the Initiated is the real inner truth (haqiqat), the hidden perfection, of the Seal of the Prophets. … Just as the Seal of the Prophets, as the form in which the divine Name “the Merciful” becomes visible, brought Mercy to both worlds and gathered into himself all the diverse figures of the cycle of prophecy, so the Seal of the Initiated becomes the form in which universal Compassion appears.

For the child is the secret of his father—in other words, the Twelfth Imam is the Prophet's secret. The Seal of the Initiated therefore gathers into himself all the diverse figures of the cycle of initiation. The happiness of both worlds will lie in following him. … For he will not destroy the many different things that exist. He will overcome their divisions by revealing the hidden laws of their unity.

If the Seal of the Initiated, the Seal of Muhammadan walayat, reveals the inner meaning of the Seal of the Prophets—or, more precisely, is himself the inner meaning of the last Prophet's mission—then the two must share a single, underlying reality. With the cycle of initiation, the greater cycle, which contains both cycles, comes full circle.

Yet its end is also its beginning: the eternal Muhammadan Reality (haqiqat-e mohammadi). Lahiji tries to picture this relationship in a diagram inspired by the very words of The Rose Garden of Mystery, on which he is commenting. In this diagram, the whole cycle of prophecy and initiation corresponds to one cosmic day and night.

The image of a cosmic Day and Night, unfolding with the revolution of the highest heavenly sphere, follows naturally when we consider the eternal Muhammadan Reality. It is the first definite reality to emerge from what has no determinate form at all (see Chapter Five above). It is the supreme Spirit, the universal Intelligence, a subtle fullness of primordial praise, also called the Muhammadan Light (Nur mohammadi). Each divine Name has its own form of manifestation and its own worshipper. In the same way, the eternal Muhammadan Reality corresponds to the supreme Name: the divine Name that gathers all the other Names into itself.

As Sadoddin Hamuyeh explains, precisely because it bears this supreme Name, the eternal Reality must appear in two distinct forms (mazhar). One is prophecy, embodied in the Seal of the Prophets. The other is initiation, embodied in the Twelfth Imam, the invisible master of the present age. Hamuyeh's disciple Aziz Nasafi puts it this way:

Thousands of prophets who came before contributed, one after another, to establishing the form in which prophecy appears; Muhammad brought it to completion. Now the time has come for initiation to appear, and to reveal the inner realities. And the Initiator in whom initiation takes visible form is the Imam, the lord of this age.
These are the two manifestations of the highest world. Each has its own nature, and together they correspond to the phases of day and night in the world we can see.

While the sun is beneath the Earth, night covers the Earth. When the sun rises toward the eastern horizon, still unseen, the darkness caused by the Earth standing in the way of its light begins to lift from things. Dawn has come, though the full brightness of morning has not. The horizon is the circle that divides the visible part of the sky from the invisible part, as seen from where we stand. It is in relation to this circle that we speak of sunrise and sunset.

From its rising point in the east, the sun climbs through successive heights until it reaches the zenith. Once it has crossed the meridian, the movement of the highest heavenly sphere begins to carry it downward; the decisive moment is marked by the midday prayer (namaz-e pishin). At last, when a lengthening shadow begins to give each thing a second outline, evening advances and the sun returns to hiding, until another morning comes.

This is a faithful image of what happens beyond the world of the senses in the complete cycle of prophecy and initiation. Prophecy is the sunrise of the Muhammadan Light, ascending from prophet to prophet until it reaches the meridian in the Seal of Prophecy. At that very point begins the cycle of initiation: the gradual descent into the night of hidden spiritual meaning, with all the trials that such a night brings in a hostile world.
Yet there is no other path. It is the necessary journey toward the morning of Resurrection, Yawm al-Qiyamat.

The prophets differed from one another as individual people, with their own lives and forms. Adam, Noah, Moses, and Jesus were not Muhammad; neither were the 124,000 nabis who were prophets without also being messengers entrusted with a new religious law.

Yet in the eternal reality of what they were (haqiqat, or ousia), all were forms in which the same Muhammadan Light appeared. Until the cycle of prophecy finally ended, that Light—like the Ebionites' Verus Propheta, the True Prophet—revealed itself through each earlier prophet, beginning with Adam, who was its eastern horizon, its sunrise.

We must therefore read the story of the prophets as the rise of prophetic consciousness: the successive heights reached by this sun on its way to the meridian. Each prophet revealed one particular perfection of the eternal Muhammadan Reality. At sunrise, a person's shadow is long. As the sun rises, the shadow grows shorter. At the zenith, the people and figures beneath it cast no shadow. In the same way, in each age and generation, the sun of the Muhammadan Reality revealed the form and shadow of a Perfect One (kamil). Those shadows marked the successive stages of the sun's ascent. When the light of prophecy reached its zenith with the appearance of the last prophet, it was noon: every shadow had vanished.

Once the Seal of the Prophets had brought this light to its zenith, humanity stood beneath it like people living on the equator at noon. Our authors explain this image in several ways. Each brings us back to a problem that their spiritual theology must constantly confront: how to avoid two opposite extremes.

We might say, for example, that the Seal of Prophecy stands at the point of perfect balance—an equinoctial line—between the day of unity and the night of multiplicity. On one side lies the danger of an abstract and all-embracing monotheism that cannot recognize the many ways God's Names become visible. On the other lies a polytheism that sees the many forms but misses the unity within them.

This is a vision that unites by distinguishing, and distinguishes by uniting. It also gives perfect balance to outward and inner meaning, and therefore to prophecy and initiation. As we have seen, keeping that balance is a central concern of Twelver Shiite thinkers when they explain the relationship between the Prophet and the Imams. They also seek balance between tashbih and tanzih: on one side, the tendency of literal-minded believers to imagine God in human form; on the other, the effort of some philosophers and theologians to preserve God's utter transcendence by stripping away every positive description. In taking this second path, they risk reducing God to an abstraction.

Shiite divine wisdom finds a path between these dangers through the idea of theophany: a manifestation of God (zohur, tajalli). This preserves both unity and multiplicity. God can appear in a human form as an image appears in a mirror, without becoming embodied in that form any more than the reflected person actually enters the glass. The same principle applies to the visions of God's Friends, whether they occur in dreams or while awake (see above, p. 269). It also applies when these Friends themselves are called manifestations of the eternal Muhammadan Reality. Lahiji gives us further striking images to make the point.

The idea of divine manifestation avoids two traps at once. We need not conclude, as a strict rationalism might, that God cannot be known at all. Nor need we make the divine into a material thing, subject to the ordinary facts studied by sociology and history. The unknowable God appears through forms of manifestation. Only through these forms does God become knowable, yet God always remains beyond them. In one sense, the form that reveals God is truly one with what it reveals (zahir and mazhar). Seen in its true spiritual reality (haqiqat), it is entirely light.
But seen as a particular, limited form, it is also shadow—the boundary that any manifestation must have if it is to appear at all.

That is why the author of The Rose Garden of Mystery cries out, “O Light of God, divine Shadow!” His words express one of the great themes developed by several Sufi masters: the shining Night, the “midnight sun,” the black Light, and the dark Noon. This, too, is a way to describe the position of the Seal of the Prophets at the point of balance. The image leads naturally to another set of symbols: the cosmic North, the direction of the heavenly Earth, the world of real spiritual images called the imaginal world (mundus imaginalis, alam al-mithal).

Thus the qibla—the direction of prayer—of the Seal of the Prophets is said to face neither East nor West, but to lie between them. It is equally distant from purely inner and purely outward religion, and equally distant from abstract monotheism and the claim that God becomes physically embodied in the world.

And so the sun of the prophetic Reality has reached the full light of noon. It emerged from hiding in the Land of Mystery and rose through the successive levels of divine manifestation, each represented by the life of a prophet. Now it has reached its zenith. The point occupied by the Seal of Prophecy both separates and joins the arc of prophecy to the arc of initiation. It is the barzakh, the meeting place or threshold between them. Together, these two arcs form the complete Cycle.

As the sun begins to descend from the zenith toward the west, shadows return and lengthen. The world necessarily enters the night of hidden spiritual meaning. The final, complete manifestation has taken place, and humanity can expect no further prophet. As we have already observed, Shiism responds to this teaching about the end of prophecy with a feeling that is less triumphant than deeply moving, even sorrowful. The Imam who completes the company of Twelve is no longer visible to ordinary human eyes.

The cycle of initiation is now the age of the Imam's concealment. He is the master of this age (sahib al-zaman) precisely because he is its sign. In the darkness, hostile powers threaten the vulnerable human lives of God's Friends, the pilgrims who must make their way through the night. It is the “Night of Destiny,” lasting until the dawn of Resurrection—the Imam's appearance. No one can avoid this night. And there is only one way to pass through it unharmed.

One conviction guides the Shiite believer through the night. The cycle of initiation, the cycle of walayat that forms prophecy's inner meaning, corresponds exactly to the cycle of prophecy. This is because prophecy is itself the outward face of walayat, or initiation. Every stage in the ascent of Day, along the eastern half of the circle, has its counterpart in the descent of Night, along the western half.

Each prophet, as one particular manifestation of the original Muhammadan Reality, revealed a quality that the Seal of Prophecy eventually gathered into a single fullness. Similarly, each initiate (wali), each Friend of God, reveals in a particular way one aspect of the perfection of the Perfect Human Being: the Seal of God's Friends, the Seal of the Initiated, the Hidden Imam of this age.
Facing each prophet on the opposite arc stands one or more of God's Friends: each eastern point has a western counterpart. Lahiji writes:

On the ascending arc and the descending arc, a figure from among the prophets and a figure from among God's Friends face one another. In the same way, every point on the western side of a circle faces and corresponds to a point on the eastern side.

This correspondence explains why Shiite authors take particular care to show the parallel between Christ, who came immediately before the Seal of the Prophets, and the First Imam of the Muhammadan age, Ali ibn Abi Talib, who came immediately after the last Prophet.

We will have reason to examine these parallels between ideas about Christ and Shiite teachings about the Imams. One especially striking illustration seems to occur in a dream of Princess Narkes, the mother of the Twelfth Imam (see Book Seven below).

That first conviction leads to a second, which gives inner strength to every believer facing the trials of this age. From one generation to the next, the hidden order of God's Friends forms a kind of spiritual knighthood, a community invisible to physical sight. At its summit stands the small company of immediate companions of the Hidden Imam (see Chapter Three, section 4, above). Very few people know of their existence, or recognize them.

Yet without them, the rest of humanity could not even continue to exist. Through them, generation after generation, there is a continual selection of “superhuman” beings: an ascent from the humanity of Adam toward the angelic humanity represented by the supreme spiritual Pole, the Hidden Imam.
Their names are the Imam's secret: “My Friends dwell beneath my tabernacles; no one knows them but me.”

Yet walayat calls each believer to make this relationship real within the hidden depths of his or her own being. The believer's relationship to the Imam, the Seal of God's Friends, should mirror that of the prophets to the Seal of Prophecy. To live that relationship personally is to move through the Night with confidence—and to bring the Night itself nearer to the dawn of the Resurrector, the Qa'im.

We have already seen what it means to establish such a relationship: to know the Imam “of one's own age.” And there can be no knowledge of the Imam without self-knowledge. Countless experiences reported across the centuries testify to this connection and to the mysterious presence of the figure at the heart of Shiite devotion: the Twelfth Imam, the “Expected Imam,” “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful.” His name is never spoken without the ritual blessing: “May God hasten for us the joy of his coming!”

The theme of the Hidden Imam, with which this work will conclude in Book Seven, truly crowns Shiite teaching about the Imams. As we have already seen, the sense that a permanent prophetic religion still lives in this world leads certain Shiite writers, among them Haydar Amoli, to identify the Twelfth Imam, the “Expected Imam,” with the Paraclete promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John.

The Paraclete—the Comforter, the Defender—thus takes on a prophetic radiance within this Shiite understanding, a significance that the scholarly study of religion has so far overlooked. This identification of the Imam with the Paraclete gives us a final and especially powerful example of what the sayings of the Imams teach about Shiism as a lived spiritual experience. It is a religion of walayat, and therefore a religion of love. For it is only through the particular form of a person's love that genuine self-knowledge becomes possible. A person comes to know himself by knowing his Imam, the “soul of his soul.” Through that knowledge he discovers himself in the form of his love—and that love is the very form of his being.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
Chapter VII What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
1. Shiism as a Religion of Spiritual Love and a Path to Self-Knowledge
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The preceding pages, especially the end of the last chapter, have already shown us where to look for the meaning of the Imam in Shiite spiritual life. One word has appeared again and again: walayat. We have seen that Shiism is, at heart, a religion of walayat. We have also begun to see why no single word in a European language can fully express it. It describes a distinctly Shiite relationship with many sides.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Yet the settings in which we have met the term tell us something essential. So does its usual Persian equivalent, dusti, and the Arabic words that sometimes accompany or replace it—hibb, mahabbat, and mawaddat. All point towards the same basic meaning: a religion of spiritual love.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Our authors often make the connection explicit. Walayat, they say, is mahabbat: devoted love. A wali is a muhibb: a friend, someone who loves. We lose that direct and deeply felt meaning when we routinely translate wali as “saint.” There are certainly points of overlap.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

But wali and walayat reach well beyond what European languages usually mean by “saint” and “sainthood,” whether in everyday speech or in formal religious usage. Perhaps it is no surprise, then, that the heart of Shiism has so often been misunderstood. Walayat is its central idea. Its different meanings extend across the whole of the Shiite view of the world, and we must begin by understanding what lies at its core.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The Imams themselves taught their followers to understand Shiism as devotion grounded in love. I want to draw together what that means, and how it shapes the Shiite understanding of human life and destiny. When Islam is understood as a religion of love, the Imam is not an optional addition: his place becomes essential.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

At the same time, we encounter the central question of Sufism—and find it raised, confronted, and answered without yet having to speak of Sufism at all. This, as I have suggested, is the key to a spiritual situation that has received too little attention. Ultimately, the Imam's meaning for the individual believer is found within walayat itself. Loving the Imam becomes a path through which the believer is led towards self-knowledge. Once that knowledge begins to open, the believer understands why love of God cannot be separated from love of the Imam.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” becomes something that can be discovered and tested through the experience of love. Then the many descriptions of the Imams in the traditions take on their full meaning. They guide the believer towards the “Soul of the soul” (jan-e jan): the Imam. I have discussed elsewhere how this understanding of the Imam becomes a lived spiritual experience in Ismailism. Here I will focus on Twelver Shiism.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Let us begin with an important point. To describe Islam as a religion of love is hardly what many people expect, especially when they think of Sunni Islam as a religion centred on religious law and the observance of the sharia. People are generally willing to speak of love in Islam when they are speaking of Sufism.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Yet Shiite Islam itself, without any special appeal to Sufism, presents itself as the religion of walayat. Evidence for this fills Shiite literature. It is brought together with particular care in a monumental work we have already encountered: Prolegomena to the Shiite Interpretation of the Qur'an, written in seventeenth-century Isfahan by Abu'l-Hasan Sharif Isfahani, a student of the great theologian Muhammad Baqir Majlisi. This work contains an extensive collection of sayings of the Prophet and the Imams, together with commentaries on them. They present walayat as the inward, hidden meaning (batin) of the Qur'anic revelation. Walayat certainly helps explain the unfolding of sacred history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
But it also shapes the believer's inner life. According to Shiite teaching, a religious act has true value only when it springs from an intention of love.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Consider the well-known tradition we have already quoted several times. One Imam after another says that upholding their cause is so demanding that only an angel close to God, a prophet sent by God, or a believer whose heart God has tested for faith can bear it. Our author stresses what this and similar sayings mean: the threefold declaration of faith—God's oneness, the Prophet's revelation, and the spiritual guidance of the Imams—cannot be fully accepted without intense longing (shawq), wholehearted assent, and perfect love (mahabbat kamila) for the complete purity (ismat) of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Indeed, the commitment to this love, to walayat, takes precedence over every obligation of the sharia. Love is what makes the fulfilment of those obligations spiritually valid; and when a person falls short, love can make up for that failure. Many sayings of the Imams make this point. One declares: “The first thing a person is asked about after death is his love for Us. If he held fast to this love (walayat) and died holding fast to it, then God accepts his prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and pilgrimage.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
“But if he did not have this love, God accepts none of his deeds.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

In Shiite ethics, then, actions must arise from the innermost self—from the batin. Prayer, good deeds, and religious duties must grow out of love, or they are empty formalities. Abu'l-Hasan Sharif writes: “Our shaykh”—meaning Muhammad Baqir Majlisi—“states this explicitly in his Bihar al-Anwar: all the Imamis agree that deeds have spiritual validity and are accepted by God only on condition of faith (iman). And an essential part of faith is love for the Twelve Imams and recognition of their spiritual authority.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Nothing could be further from a religion defined solely by its laws. The implications for Shiite Islam's place in the world reach very far. We therefore need to understand exactly why the Imam is the focus of this love. And when we speak simply of “the Imam,” the name can mean each of the Twelve or all Fourteen Immaculate Ones together. Because they share one essential reality, each is, in this sense, also all the others.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Let me explain more fully, building on what we have seen so far. Whatever we know of God is, necessarily, knowledge of God as it is given to human beings. This is true of what we discover through our own efforts, but just as true of what the hidden God (Deus absconditus) reveals of himself as the revealed God (Deus revelatus). Even revelations given to prophets reach us as knowledge intended for human understanding. The saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” expresses this human dimension of our knowledge of God.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

But how can we move from knowing ourselves to knowing our Lord? According to the teaching we are examining, we can do so only because the Imam is the form in which self-knowledge becomes possible: the point of connection between the human person and the hidden God. The saying becomes true through an inward realization of the teaching about the Imam. The Imam gives human form to what a human being can know of God.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

And recognizing the Imam—not merely one of the Twelve, but each and all of them in their eternal reality and their role as manifestations of God—protects our belief in divine oneness (tawhid) from two opposite errors. One is ta'til, denying that God can be known through any of the qualities we speak of. The other is tashbih, making God resemble the things we know. Simple believers and sophisticated theologians alike can fall into either trap without realizing it.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

We have already met the first danger, ta'til. To avoid speaking of God in merely human terms, it places the divine reality altogether beyond human language and understanding. Shiism also teaches that God transcends every name and quality that human language can express.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

But if we stop there, we are left with no knowledge of God at all. We have lost the personal relationship between God and humanity that faith requires. The opposite error is to treat God's utterly transcendent essence as though it possessed the very names and qualities we give it. That is tashbih: describing God too much in our own image. Someone might object: “Why do I need the Imam? God is enough for me. I need no one between God and myself.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

But the speaker forgets something basic. The God of whom we speak directly is always God as revealed to us—God as known through the form in which God makes himself known. Even when we describe God as beyond all personal identity, we speak on the basis of what is shown to us, or withheld from us.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Without some form of manifestation—a mazhar, a form through which God appears—we could not speak of God at all. This manifestation is what is called the “Face” of God. We have already seen how important this idea is in Shiism, and have been told that the Imam is this Face. Later we shall see that the Imam is also described as the one “placed before” the believer, the one who “walks ahead of his very being” (moqaddam ala wujudi-hi).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

If we lose this understanding of the Imam, we also lose the grounds on which our human knowledge of God—or God's revelation to humanity—can be trusted. Then we are caught between the same two mistakes. We may dismiss that knowledge as merely human and end up unable to say anything about God (ta'til). Or we may accept our human descriptions without recognizing what they really are, and turn them into images of God that we mistake for God himself (tashbih).
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Only the Imam, understood as the person through whom God is revealed, protects the truth in our human knowledge while carrying us beyond its merely human limits. This helps explain why certain Sufi masters outside Shiism wrestled so intensely with the tension between these two dangers. They were trying to preserve tawhid: the recognition that God is One.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Yet the mystery of God's oneness is the mystery of divine solitude—“God alone is alone.” We are not speaking of the number one standing above countless other separate beings. We are speaking of the mystery by which each unique being is unique: the One appearing in endlessly many ways without ceasing to be the One.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The Face of God that remains uniquely present for each unique being is, in this teaching, the Imam. That is what the Imams express through the many names and descriptions they give themselves in their sayings. Shiite prayers draw on these names throughout a complex religious calendar. A commentary on a single prayer can therefore become an entire study of the Imam and what he means. We have already seen one such example.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The love directed towards the Imam is universal. So too is the Imam's role in making God's revelation meaningful to human beings. Without him, there could be no authentic understanding of divine oneness. Together, these ideas explain what we might call the universal outlook of Shiism: its belief that all the prophets, and everyone who has truly followed them, belong to one continuing religion of love. It embraces the spiritual descendants of Abraham throughout humanity's sacred history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

Every prophet and every true follower has professed this same walayat. They make up one vast spiritual body—the corpus mysticum. Ismaili writers, for their part, speak of the “Temple of Light” of the Imamate. To reject this bond of love would, in this understanding, also be to reject the prophetic revelations that came before Islam.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

The Second Imam, Hasan ibn Ali, declares: “Whoever denies the supreme standing of the Commander of the Faithful [Ali, the First Imam] contradicts the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, the writings of Abraham, and every other Book that God has sent down from heaven. For after the witness to God's oneness (tawhid) and to the mission of the prophets, the most important testimony in all these Books is the recognition of walayat towards Ali and the Imams.”
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life

This follows from another saying we already know. The Prophet declares that the Imam was sent secretly with every earlier prophet, but was sent openly with him, the Seal of the Prophets. Walayat—the divine love given to the full company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—is the inward secret of every revelation entrusted to the prophets. It is the secret of the Hidden Treasure that longs to be known. The Imam is that Treasure becoming knowable and capable of being loved. Christian theologians have asked how people living before the historical event of Redemption could have been saved, given that Redemption took place at a particular moment in history.
VII. What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life
But we are beginning to see why the question cannot be framed in quite that way within a prophetic religion understood as continuous from Adam to the final Imam.
